Dear young owner,

My niece showed me the reviews of your little restaurant on her phone. A countryside shop serving food from six countries? I had to write.

I'm Malai. I've run a kitchen in Bangkok for thirty years, but I started at my mother's street stall, frying holy basil pork for taxi drivers at two in the morning. They had no time, only hunger, and this dish never let them down.

Hot wok, lots of garlic and chili, and the basil goes in last. A fried egg on top, crispy at the edges. That's the whole secret.

Someone who cooks for strangers deserves a good everyday dish.

Dear owner,

It's Malai again. I hear the basil pork is doing well. Good!

Pad Thai is the dish every visitor asks me for, so you should have it too. When I was young I thought it was too simple to be proud of. Then a tourist cried at my table because it reminded her of her honeymoon. Simple food carries big memories.

Soak the noodles, don't boil them. Shrimp, tofu, egg, then the sauce: tamarind, fish sauce, palm sugar. Bean sprouts at the very end so they stay crisp.

Don't let anyone tell you a small shop can't be a great one.

Dear owner,

Malai again. You have come so far!

Khao soi comes from the north, from Chiang Mai, where I went alone at twenty after my first restaurant failed. I thought my career was over. An old woman at a noodle stall fed me every day and refused my money. "Pay me when you are a chef," she said.

Coconut curry broth, chicken, soft egg noodles with crispy noodles on top, pickled greens and lime on the side.

I went back ten years later to pay her. Failure was not the end of my story. It won't be the end of yours either.

Dear owner,

Malai here. Your shop's reputation is growing! My niece shows me new reviews every week.

Today, something sweet. Bua loy was my mother's medicine for every sadness. Bad grades, broken toys, a broken heart: she rolled little balls of sticky rice dough and floated them in warm coconut milk.

Mix glutinous rice flour with mashed pumpkin and taro for color. Roll them small. Simmer in coconut milk with sugar and a pinch of salt.

Rolling them is slow work. Use the time to breathe.

Kenji again. I hope the gyudon has found its way to tired people.

After I left my office job, I trained for six years in a ramen shop. My master barely spoke. He corrected me by tasting my broth and pouring it away. I hated it. Later I understood: he was not angry. He was teaching me a patience I did not have.

Pork bones simmered for many hours, noodles, a soft egg, spring onion. The broth cannot be rushed.

If working with others ever hurt you, that is all right. A kitchen can be a quiet place to heal.

Kenji. People online say your shop has become a place to rest. I am glad.

Tonkatsu reminds me of my father. He was strict, and we rarely talked. But on exam days he would fry a pork cutlet for me, because "katsu" sounds like "to win." He never said good luck. The cutlet said it for him.

Pound the pork, then flour, egg, and breadcrumbs. Fry until golden and crisp. Serve with shredded cabbage.

Some people cannot say what they feel. Food can.

To the owner,

Kenji. Your shop is known even among cooks here now. Truly.

Tempura is the hardest dish I know. The batter must be cold and barely mixed, lumps and all. The oil must be exactly right. For years mine came out heavy and oily, and I wanted to quit.

The trick is to stop trying so hard. Mix less. Touch less. Trust the heat.

Shrimp, pumpkin, sweet potato, a light flour batter, fried quickly until it crackles.

I think people are the same. They don't need to be perfect. They need to be light enough to breathe.

I am Kenji Morita. Before I became a cook, I worked in an office in Osaka. I was not good with people. Every night I ate gyudon alone at a counter, and that bowl was the kindest thing in my day.

Thin beef simmered with onion in soy sauce and a little sweetness, over hot rice, pickled ginger on the side.

Quick, warm, honest. Please make it for someone who is tired.

Hello,

A traveler who ate at your shop left a long review online. He said the food tasted like someone cared. That is rare, so I am writing.

My name is Lin Wei. My grandfather ran a teahouse, and the first thing he ever let me cook was fried rice made from yesterday's rice. He said, "Fresh rice is for the rich. Day-old rice is for the clever."

Shrimp, a little ham, egg, and rice that has dried out overnight. Keep the fire high and keep your hand moving.

Nothing wasted, everything shared. That is a good way to run a kitchen.

Lin Wei writing. I read that your shop now has regulars. That is when a restaurant truly begins.

In my grandfather's teahouse, the whole family folded dumplings together every morning before dawn. As a boy I was too slow, and my pleats were ugly. My aunt said, "Ugly dumplings taste the same. Keep folding."

Pork, shrimp, cabbage, a little ginger, wrapped in thin dough and steamed until the skin turns clear.

You fold alone for now. One day, perhaps, someone will fold beside you.

Hello, my friend,

May I call you that now? Lin Wei here.

Mooncakes are for the Mid-Autumn Festival, when families gather under the full moon. For many years I worked abroad and spent the festival alone. Every year, my grandfather mailed me a single mooncake, wrapped so carefully it never broke.

Sweet red bean paste with a salted egg yolk in the center, like the moon, wrapped in thin pastry and pressed in a mold.

Distance does not break a family. Neither does silence. Send something warm to someone you miss.

Your shop is famous now, but I hope you remember why you started. You cook so that strangers feel at home. That is worth celebrating.
